newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says car crash diplomat had previous record.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says car crash diplomat had previous record.

text.p: The Georgian diplomat involved in a car crash that killed a 16-year-old girl has been accused of other traffic violations in Washington, D.C. and Virginia over the past year or two, the State Department said on Monday.
Georgy Makharadze "had received traffic violations not just in the District but, I believe, in Virginia over the last year or two," spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.

Burns was unable to describe the number and nature of those violations and said the department was not even sure it had been informed by local police authorities about all the incidents in which Makharadze may have been involved.
Nevertheless, he insisted the State Department "does follow very carefully the activities of foreign diplomats in the United States from this perspective."

In the past four years, the State Department took away the driving licenses of 37 diplomats who had showed a pattern of "irresponsible" driving behaviour, including speeding, drunken driving, accidents and parking tickets, he said.
Eight diplomats were expelled since 1992 for drunk driving.
But Burns said Makharadze's license was not among those lifted and he was uncertain whether the diplomat had demonstrated a particularly "egregious" record.

The U.S. attorney's office said last week it believed it had sufficient evidence to prosecute Makharadze over the January 3 five-car smash that killed Joviane Waltrick, a 16-year-old Brazilian girl living in Kensington, Maryland.
But charges have not yet been filed. The U.S. attorney's office may first bring the case to a grand jury.

Diplomats normally escape prosecution in such instances because they are protected by diplomatic immunity. But Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze announced he was prepared to lift Makharadze's diplomatic immunity so he can face charges.

"Frankly, it was with grave feelings and a heavy heart that I made the decision regarding the fate of the young and doubtlessly talented diplomat, Shevardnadze said in a statement released on Sunday. But "I cannot imagine diplomacy and politics devoid of moral principle."

Burns said the State Department regularly receives police reports on the driving records of foreign diplomats in the United States, but may be only getting a sampling of the incidents that are occurring.

Secretary of State Warren Christopher "is very concerned that we redouble our efforts to make sure that the local police departments are giving us timely and full reports on any serious violations of the law incurred by ... foreign diplomats here in the Washington area," he said.
